claims.claim: Metformin is the first-line pharmacologic therapy for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
Metformin is recommended as the initial agent for type 2 diabetes.
Metformin has demonstrated significant reductions in HbA1c compared with placebo.
Metformin has demonstrated significant reductions in fasting glucose compared with placebo.
Metformin has a favorable safety profile.
Metformin has benefits for weight.
Metformin has benefits for cardiovascular outcomes.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) significantly delayed albuminuria progression in people with type 2 diabetes (risk ratio 0.71; 95 % CI 0.66-0.76).
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) improved long-term estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared with placebo.
Combined SGLT2i and GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy did not show a significant additional benefit for major adverse kidney events.
The evidence supports a renoprotective effect of SGLT2i alone.
Meta-analyses demonstrate that exercise improves blood-sugar control in type 2 diabetes.
Aerobic exercise alone or combined with resistance training lowers HbA1c by about 0.5 %.
Aerobic exercise alone or combined with resistance training improves glycaemic markers.
In type 2 diabetes, exercise reduces HbA1c by ~0.48 %.
In type 2 diabetes, exercise reduces fasting glucose.
Metformin alone is more effective than exercise alone in reducing HbA1c.
Combined exercise and metformin yields even greater reductions in HbA1c and fasting glucose.
Mixed-modality programs improve glucose metabolism.
Mixed-modality programs improve insulin sensitivity.
Regular exercise is an effective non-pharmacologic strategy for improving blood-sugar control in type 2 diabetes.
Antihypertensive therapy (AHT) is commonly started.
The effect of AHT on cerebral blood flow is modest in those aged 50-70 years.
AHT may increase cerebral blood flow only in those aged >70 years.
Nurse-led, community-based programs improve long-term BP control.

Nurse-led, community-based programs show a modest benefit over usual care.
Group-delivered interventions reduce systolic BP by about 7 mmHg compared with usual care.
Group-delivered interventions reduce diastolic BP by about 5 mmHg compared with usual care.
Deprescribing antihypertensives in frail or multimorbid older adults has uncertain effects on mortality.

AHT initiation or augmentation lowers the prevalence of orthostatic hypotension.

Monitoring for orthostatic symptoms is needed when AHT is initiated or augmented.

Lowering dietary sodium reduces blood pressure.

In patients on dialysis, salt restriction caused a 4.4 mmHg drop in diastolic blood pressure.
In non-dialysis CKD, low-salt diets lowered clinic systolic blood pressure by 4.9 mmHg.
In non-dialysis CKD, low-salt diets lowered ambulatory systolic blood pressure by 5.9 mmHg.
In non-dialysis CKD, low-salt diets lowered clinic diastolic blood pressure by 2.3 mmHg.
In non-dialysis CKD, low-salt diets lowered ambulatory diastolic blood pressure by 3.0 mmHg.

Weight loss achieved through metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) reduces asthma symptoms and medication use.
